title: How to Spot a Bad Argument in Two Seconds
subtitle: Most persuasion that fools us isn't lying about facts — it's cheating on logic. Learn the common cheats and you can't be conned the same way twice.
hook: A claim can be built from true facts and still be rubbish — because the *reasoning* is broken. These broken moves are **logical fallacies**, and the same handful show up in every heated argument, ad, and comment section. Learn to name them and something clicks: you start seeing the cheat in real time, mid-sentence. Today: your bad-argument detector.

sections.heading: Valid vs. true
sections.body: Two different things. An argument is **valid** if the conclusion *follows* from the premises. It's **sound** only if it's valid *and* the premises are actually true. Fallacies are usually failures of validity dressed up to feel convincing — the words flow, the logic doesn't. Spotting them is about checking the *shape* of the argument, not just the facts.

sections.heading: The greatest hits
items: Ad hominem — attacking the person, not their argument ('you would say that, you're X').
Straw man — beating up a weaker, distorted version of what someone said.
False dilemma — 'you're either with us or against us' (pretending only two options exist).
Appeal to authority — 'an expert said so' as proof (experts can be wrong or off-topic).
Slippery slope — claiming one small step must inevitably lead to disaster, with no link shown.

sections.caption: The check: do the premises actually support the conclusion (valid)? And are the premises true (sound)? Fallacies fail the first test.

sections.label: The meta-move
sections.body: When something *feels* persuasive but you can't say why, pause and ask: 'What's the actual claim, and does the evidence given actually support it?' Nine times out of ten the persuasion was riding on a fallacy or a bias (yesterday's lesson) rather than real support. Naming the move breaks the spell.

sections.caption: Ten common logical fallacies, explained with examples.

takeaways: **Valid** = conclusion follows; **sound** = valid AND premises true. Fallacies fail validity.
Know the greats: **ad hominem, straw man, false dilemma, appeal to authority, slippery slope**.
A claim built from true facts can still be a bad argument if the logic is broken.
Check the *shape*: do the premises actually support the conclusion?
Persuasion that 'feels right' but you can't justify is usually a fallacy or a bias.

quiz.q: 'You can't trust his economics argument — he's rich.' Which fallacy?
quiz.explain: Ad hominem: attacking the person instead of the argument.

quiz.q: What's the difference between valid and sound?
options: Valid = conclusion follows; sound = valid AND premises are true
quiz.explain: Validity is about structure; soundness adds that the premises are actually true.

quiz.q: CALLBACK: How do fallacies relate to yesterday's cognitive biases?
options: Biases are how our brain slips; fallacies are the broken argument-shapes that exploit those slips
quiz.explain: A straw man or false dilemma lands because System 1 doesn't check the logic. Biases (internal) and fallacies (in the argument) are two sides of the same weakness.

tg_quiz.q: 'Either we ban this completely or society collapses.' Which fallacy?
tg_quiz.correct: Yep — false dilemma: pretending only two options exist.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's a false dilemma — it fakes an either/or when more options exist.
tg_quiz.explain: Real choices rarely come in just two flavors.
